lesson_title: The Pencil That Lights a Bulb
hook_text: Clip a pencil lead into a circuit and the bulb lights. Carbon is a non-metal. So what is going on?
clip_script: A torch bulb, a cell, two wires and a gap. Clip a copper wire into the gap: the bulb blazes. Iron nail: on. Aluminium foil: on. Metals are shiny, they flatten when you hammer them, they stretch into wire, and they let electricity and heat flow straight through. Now a lump of sulfur: nothing. It is dull, it shatters when you hit it, and it blocks the current. That is a non-metal. Now a pencil lead. Carbon, a non-metal. The bulb lights. Graphite is the great exception, a non-metal that conducts. Its cousin diamond, also pure carbon, does not conduct at all; same atoms, different arrangement. Last, a chip of silicon: shiny like a metal, shatters like a non-metal, and the bulb barely glows. That in-between behaviour, a semiconductor, is why silicon runs every phone and every solar panel on every roof. Shine, bend, conduct: three tests, three personalities.
visual_style: A simple whiteboard circuit with a gap; samples drop into the gap one by one and the bulb lights, stays dark or glows faintly, with a hammer icon flattening copper and shattering sulfur.
pacing: Rapid sample-by-sample rhythm with a pause and reveal on the pencil lead.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and classify any element by its personality.
